Packing & Loading

How to Load a Moving Truck Safely and Efficiently

Plan the order, balance the weight, protect the furniture, and secure each section before the truck moves.

Author: Ralph Ivey

Last updated: 2026-08-10

Experience: Written for working trucking and moving businesses.

How to load a moving truck

  1. Check the limits first. Read the truck's payload information and never exceed its rated capacity. Account for passengers, fuel, equipment, and cargo.
  2. Stage before loading. Separate heavy appliances and furniture, medium boxes, fragile items, mattresses, and last-on essentials so the loading order stays controlled.
  3. Build a stable front wall. Put dense, sturdy items low and toward the front of the cargo area. Keep weight balanced from left to right instead of loading one side first.
  4. Fill vertical space carefully. Use similarly sized boxes in stable columns. Keep heavy boxes low, lighter boxes higher, and avoid loose gaps that allow stacks to shift.
  5. Protect and separate. Use moving pads, corner guards, mattress bags, and stretch wrap where appropriate. Do not rely on plastic wrap alone to restrain heavy furniture.
  6. Secure each section. Use the truck's rated tie-down points and suitable straps as the load grows. Close off sections so one sudden stop cannot move the entire shipment.
  7. Finish with essentials. Load cleaning supplies, tools, an overnight box, and items needed first at delivery near the door—provided they can still be restrained safely.

Before driving

  • Confirm every door is latched and nothing blocks the roll-up door or ramp.
  • Check mirrors, lights, tires, clearance, and the route before departure.
  • Drive more slowly, brake earlier, and recheck straps after the first safe stop.
  • Follow the rental company or vehicle manufacturer's instructions whenever they differ from general guidance.

Common loading mistakes

  • Placing all heavy items on one side or at the rear.
  • Stacking heavy boxes on fragile or partially filled boxes.
  • Leaving furniture unpadded or expecting loose objects to stay in place.
  • Using damaged straps, unrated anchor points, or unsecured hand trucks and ramps.
